title: Technology: AI Presents Both Opportunity and Threat to Young Lawyers
author: Joanne Harris

dom.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source addresses AI’s effects on law-firm workflows, junior-lawyer development and training, not whether technical accuracy can confer legitimate judicial authority. Its emphasis on preserving substantive expertise overlaps with the cluster’s concern for sustained human competence, but it provides no position on autonomous adjudication, consent, challenge rights or institutional legitimacy.
qs: It also discovered that lawyers expect AI to have a ‘significant impact on law firm structure, hiring and business models.’ Training was identified as a key priority, both in terms of teaching staff about the use of AI and in respect of coaching associates on legal work to allow them to have ‘well-rooted expertise when they reach senior roles’.
He highlights that workflows are already shifting, with tasks such as document reviews now falling to AI.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: Harris accepts that AI adoption requires institutional action and materially develops the cluster’s competence theme by identifying a dual training obligation: teaching staff to use AI while preserving associates’ substantive expertise for senior-level supervision. She also qualifies broad adoption claims by locating current use mainly in back-office functions and larger organisations.

The Task Force found that AI is primarily used for back-office functions in law firms.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the core training risk: automating foundational junior work can impede skill development, so associates should first demonstrate independent legal competence and then learn responsible AI use. Its optimism about new work, wellbeing and efficiency is a caveat, not a rejection of deliberate training safeguards.
qs: He cites the example of a US-based Big Law firm, with its own proprietary AI tools, which is banning its junior lawyers from using AI so that others in the organisation can assess their performance.
The firm then expects associates to learn how to deploy AI tools responsibly for clients later on, once they have the requisite legal skills.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s claims that buyer efficiency expectations will pressure law-firm billing and that AI is more likely to reshape roles and training than eliminate the profession. Its evidence is illustrative and predictive, however, and does not directly establish that legal departments have already captured broad gains or that organisational absorption is the principal bottleneck.
qs: In-house counsel want their advisers to be efficient and cost-effective, and AI tools can help significantly with that.
Further, Paton says law firms will have to rethink their billing models as AI use becomes more prevalent.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing of AI as a training and operating-model challenge rather than simple lawyer substitution. It argues for preserving foundational transactional learning, assessing unaided legal skills before AI use, and then teaching responsible deployment, while also anticipating new work, retention benefits and billing-model change. Its claims are qualitative and predictive, consistent with the cluster’s caution that outcomes remain unsettled.

kp.k: AI becomes an operational reality for legal practice
kp.d: Harris reports that the IBA’s Legal Agenda 2025, published in December, classifies AI as a critical issue. The article frames the growing ability to automate tasks previously performed by young lawyers, interns and trainees as raising unresolved questions about job losses versus changed career paths.
qs: The IBA’s *Legal Agenda 2025*, published in December, ranks AI as a ‘critical issue’, highlighting its transition from ‘an emerging concern to a regulatory and operational reality.’
An increasing number of tasks previously undertaken by young lawyers, interns and trainees can now be carried out relatively easily by AI

kp.k: Reported adoption concentrates on back-office work
kp.d: The article reports findings from the IBA AI Task Force’s first comprehensive AI report, produced in autumn 2024: law-firm use was primarily back-office, while larger organisations had a higher percentage of client-facing use. Lawyers expected significant effects on structure, hiring and business models. The article supplies no sample sizes or adoption percentages.
qs: The Task Force found that AI is primarily used for back-office functions in law firms.
However, in larger organisations, there’s a higher percentage of AI usage in client-facing work.
It also discovered that lawyers expect AI to have a ‘significant impact on law firm structure, hiring and business models.’

kp.k: Automated junior tasks threaten foundational learning
kp.d: Sönke Lund says workflows are already shifting, with document review falling to AI. He predicts that removing this early-career work will reduce young lawyers’ exposure to legal basics, increasing law schools’ responsibility for foundational education. The Task Force likewise identifies both AI training and substantive associate development as priorities.
qs: He highlights that workflows are already shifting, with tasks such as document reviews now falling to AI.
‘This will change, so that means that the young lawyer will not have contact from the beginning with the basics.’

Training was identified as a key priority, both in terms of teaching staff about the use of AI and in respect of coaching associates on legal work to allow them to have ‘well-rooted expertise when they reach senior roles’.

kp.k: Legal education must combine analysis and responsible technology use
kp.d: Paul Paton argues that law schools must preserve fundamental analytical education while preparing students to use AI and other technologies ethically and responsibly throughout changing careers. This is a recommendation about professional preparation, not evidence that existing curricula achieve it.
qs: Paul Paton, a current officer and former Co-Chair of the IBA Alternative and New Law Business Structures Committee, agrees law schools must educate their students on the fundamentals of analysis, while also ensuring they’re equipped to work with AI and other technology.
‘That puts a responsibility on law schools to understand what new tools there are and making sure students are prepared to use them ethically and responsibly.’

kp.k: Manual practice underpins competent review of AI output
kp.d: Pranav Srivastava argues that lawyers need experience doing underlying legal work themselves to review AI output competently. He recommends training methodologies requiring manual work for an unspecified initial period, treating legal competence as a prerequisite for effective AI use.
qs: ‘I firmly believe AI is only as good as the lawyer using it,’ says Pranav Srivastava

‘For us to be able to review we have to go through the rigour of doing that work ourselves. Training methodologies will have to be established to allow lawyers to do that work manually up to a certain point of time.’

kp.k: One firm delays junior AI use for performance assessment
kp.d: Paton reports differing firm expectations and cites an unnamed US-based Big Law firm that prohibits junior AI use despite having proprietary tools, allowing others to assess juniors’ performance. Associates are expected to learn responsible client-facing deployment after acquiring legal skills. Paton treats due diligence as a developmental activity and urges firms to fill training gaps.
qs: He cites the example of a US-based Big Law firm, with its own proprietary AI tools, which is banning its junior lawyers from using AI so that others in the organisation can assess their performance.
The firm then expects associates to learn how to deploy AI tools responsibly for clients later on, once they have the requisite legal skills.

‘Doing due diligence has never been a passion project for a junior lawyer, but it is a way to learn about the transaction to build up the skills so that you can become a senior provider. That’s where firms need to work with junior lawyers to fill up the gaps,’ Paton adds.

kp.k: AI-related legal challenges may generate new demand
kp.d: Lund offers an optimistic counterpoint to displacement concerns: AI creates legal challenges and associated work concerning data and emerging legislation. This is his market-opportunity argument, not a quantified finding about new demand or net employment.
qs: ‘There’s a bright future for the legal profession because AI [creates] a lot of legal challenges,’ says Lund

‘We can convert the problem into a virtue. There’s a lot of business there in terms of data and the legislation that’s coming up now, it’s all based on these kind of problems, so it gives you a lot of work.’

kp.k: Routine-task automation could improve wellbeing and retention
kp.d: Srivastava suggests that automating mundane work could keep lawyers engaged and in the profession longer by reducing excessive hours and burnout. The article presents these benefits as his expectations rather than measured workforce outcomes.
qs: Srivastava, who’s a partner at New Delhi firm Phoenix Legal, suggests that the use of AI for mundane, routine tasks could actually be a benefit, keeping lawyers engaged and in the profession longer.
‘It is a profession where people face burnout, people face crazy work hours, [with] no semblance of having personal time, and I think AI resolves a lot of those problems,’ he says.

kp.k: Client efficiency demands put pressure on billing models
kp.d: Harris states that in-house counsel want efficient, cost-effective external advisers and that AI can assist. Paton predicts that more prevalent AI use will require firms to reconsider billing models; the article specifies neither replacement pricing arrangements nor quantified savings.
qs: In-house counsel want their advisers to be efficient and cost-effective, and AI tools can help significantly with that.
Further, Paton says law firms will have to rethink their billing models as AI use becomes more prevalent.

kp.k: Court citation problems highlight responsible-use and skills requirements
kp.d: Harris reports that courts worldwide are grappling with AI-generated case citations that relying lawyers have not identified as such, without identifying cases or error rates. Srivastava predicts prompt drafting will become as important as legal drafting; Lund stresses that AI remains a tool, and Paton urges risk awareness and ethical use across schools, firms and lawyers.
qs: This latter requirement is already proving challenging, with courts around the world grappling with case citations that have been generated by AI and that haven’t been identified as such by the lawyers relying on them.
‘AI is only as good as the prompt given to AI. Drafting prompts is going to become a skill in itself, as important as legal drafting,’ Srivastava says.
Lund agrees, adding that ‘as always, law firms have to get used to this new situation, and young lawyers have to understand that AI is only a tool.’
Paton says law schools, firms and their lawyers all need to be aware of the risks and be able to use AI responsibly and ethically.

kp.k: The article anticipates adaptation rather than professional extinction
kp.d: Harris characterises the legal community as generally not seeing AI as an existential threat, while expecting changes to professional structures and work. Her synthesis emphasises combining analytical skills with the ability to obtain useful, correct AI output and remaining alert to future developments; it is not presented as a measured consensus.
qs: The legal community, overall, doesn’t seem to believe that AI is an existential threat to the profession.
It will force adaptation in structure and in the way lawyers work, and legal professionals will have to remain vigilant to ensure they don’t get caught out by future developments.

But a good lawyer of the future will be someone who can deploy the analytical skills still being taught by universities and also be able to work with AI tools to obtain useful, correct information from them.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is shifting junior legal work, creating training challenges, and prompting changes in legal careers, client service and business models; interviewees also predict new work and better working conditions.
pts.d: Harris reports that AI can already perform an increasing number of tasks formerly undertaken by young lawyers, interns and trainees. She reports the IBA AI Task Force's findings that adoption is primarily in back-office functions, with more client-facing usage in larger organisations, and that lawyers expect substantial organisational changes. Lund says document-review workflows are already shifting to AI and predicts reduced early exposure to legal fundamentals, increasing the responsibility of law schools to teach them. Paton argues that legal education must combine analytical fundamentals with ethical, responsible technology use, and that firms must fill gaps in junior lawyers' experiential learning. Srivastava argues that lawyers need manual experience to review AI output competently and predicts that prompt drafting will become as important a skill as legal drafting. Lund predicts additional legal business from AI-related data issues and emerging legislation. Srivastava suggests automation of routine work could reduce burnout and excessive hours and improve retention. Harris says AI can help meet in-house counsel's expectations of efficiency and cost-effectiveness; Paton predicts that increasing adoption will require billing-model changes. Harris presents adaptation rather than professional extinction as the legal community's general expectation, while noting problems with AI-generated citations. Paton concludes that lawyers and institutions able to use AI responsibly should thrive. The article raises potential job losses as a question rather than providing a definite employment forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article relies on reported IBA findings, professional interview testimony, one unnamed firm's training practice and general references to court citation problems, rather than quantitative performance or employment evidence.
pts.d: Harris cites the IBA's Legal Agenda 2025 as institutional recognition of AI's operational importance and the AI Task Force's autumn 2024 report for adoption patterns, anticipated organisational impacts and training priorities. The article does not provide the report's sample, methodology or numerical adoption rates. Lund's account of changing workflows and new legal demand draws on his professional and Task Force experience. Paton offers an unnamed US Big Law firm's practice of prohibiting junior AI use initially so that their performance can be assessed, followed by responsible deployment after foundational skills develop. This is an illustrative training practice, not evidence of an industry-wide policy. Srivastava's claims about verification skills, prompting, burnout and retention are professional judgments without quantified supporting outcomes. Harris refers to courts encountering AI-generated citations that lawyers failed to identify, but supplies no named cases or measured error rates. The source offers no quantified forecast of job losses, revenue growth, cost savings or billing changes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Workflow changes and citation risks are described as current by January 2026; career, training and market predictions have no fixed horizon and are conditional on adoption and responsible use.
pts.d: The article is dated 7 January 2026, cites an autumn 2024 AI Task Force report and refers to Legal Agenda 2025 as published in December. Harris and Lund describe task automation, workflow shifts and changing client expectations as already occurring. Predictions about professional structure, new legal demand, retention and prompting skills are open-ended rather than tied to a target year. Paton's billing prediction is explicitly linked to more prevalent AI use. Srivastava's training prescription requires manual work for an unspecified initial period; the unnamed firm's approach similarly makes AI deployment contingent on acquiring requisite legal skills. Benefits to career prospects depend on retaining analytical competence, understanding outputs and using tools ethically and responsibly. Paton says firms differ in their expectations of AI knowledge, qualifying any suggestion of a uniform transition.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are junior lawyers, legal educators, law firms, corporate legal buyers and courts.
pts.d: Young lawyers, interns and trainees face automation of routine tasks and possible loss of foundational learning opportunities, alongside prospective relief from mundane work and excessive hours. Associates need sufficient legal expertise to verify AI output and progress into senior roles. Law schools face greater responsibility for analytical fundamentals and technology preparation; firms must redesign training and may change staffing, hiring and billing models. Larger organisations are reported to use AI more often in client-facing work, while the unnamed proprietary-tool example concerns a US Big Law firm specifically. Lawyers advising on data and AI-related legislation may gain new work, according to Lund. In-house counsel are the buyer-side group seeking more efficient and cost-effective advice. Courts and clients are affected when lawyers rely on inadequately checked AI-generated citations. The article does not quantify impacts by jurisdiction or firm size, beyond the reported adoption distinction.
